rows.text: Honestly, the sign-in and workspace setup looks simpler than half of what my team wrestles with in Vault, so I could get through this without a training deck. My worry is the dossier creation step — I'm expected to already know a dossier ID in a specific format, and half my clients are pre-filing and don't have one yet. If there's no path for "Health Canada hasn't assigned it yet," I'm stuck at the front door.

Mechanically, yes, my team could sign in and create a dossier — it's simpler than Veeva's login, frankly. But the "New dossier +" form assumes you walk in already knowing your dossier ID and its exact format, and half the time with a new client we're still waiting on that from Health Canada. There's no forgot-password link either, which with nine people on my team is a guaranteed weekly headache for me.

Honestly, the guided step-by-step flow looks easier than what my juniors face in docuBridge — locked steps with plain-language reasons would cut down the "what do I do next" questions I get daily. But I've done hundreds of sequences; a linear wizard could feel like handcuffs when I need to jump around, prep Module 3 in parallel, or fix something out of order. The 3D "Submission tower" is a gimmick I'd ignore.

For me personally, the guided ten-step rail would be easy — arguably too easy, since I've filed hundreds of sequences and don't need a padlock telling me why I can't touch validation yet. My worry is the reverse: my junior associates would find it simple to click through, and simplicity in this domain can mask complexity. The linear lock-step flow would actually slow my team down, because in real life we work Modules 2 through 5 in parallel while the admin data is still settling.

For me personally, the flow itself looks simple enough — one button, two fields, click a tile. My concern isn't the clicking, it's that the form assumes I already have the dossier ID in hand; my coordinators would be toggling between this and an email from OSIP to find it. A browser confirm dialog for deleting an entire dossier and all its documents is far too casual for something my team could hit by accident.

Honestly, this looks simpler than half of what my team fights with in Vault — one button, two fields, and you're into Module 1. My worry is the flip side of that simplicity: my coordinators live in bulk, and a grid of tiles with a browser confirm dialog for delete feels like a consumer app, not a regulated document system.

On paper this looks manageable — the three-panel layout mirrors what my team already knows from Vault and docuBridge, and the "req"/"opt" badges on the section tree are the kind of at-a-glance triage we currently do in Excel. My worry is the pre-filled sample data: junior associates under deadline pressure will miss a "sample" tag, and I'd need to build a QC step around that. The form-based authoring itself seems simpler than wrangling templates in Word, assuming the fields match what our SOPs require.

The three-panel layout — section tree, working panel, status rail — mirrors what my team already knows from docuBridge and Vault, so navigation itself would not be a hurdle. The forms with labeled fields look straightforward enough that even my junior associates could work through them. My worry is the "edit every field to your product" instruction; pre-filled sample data that must be manually overwritten in every field is exactly the kind of thing a tired person misses at 6 p.m. before a deadline.

Honestly, the layout sounds familiar enough — a section tree with status glyphs and req/opt badges is not far from how we track things in Vault, so my team could navigate it. What would slow us down is not knowing which sections support AI drafting until we click into each one; with 200-plus sections in a dossier, that trial-and-error hunting would drive my writers crazy.

The section tree with req/opt badges and status glyphs maps well to how my team already thinks in eCTD section numbers, so navigation would be quick. The chat drafting itself looks simple enough, but the fact that you only discover whether AI drafting exists after clicking into a section would drive my associates crazy — we'd waste clicks hunting for it across five modules.

The three-column layout with module tabs and status dots reads a lot like what my team already knows from Vault RIM, so I don't expect a steep curve for my senior people. The dossier ID format requirement would trip up every new hire — one letter plus 6-7 digits with no explanation of why. My worry is my junior associates clicking Export from that Sequences card without ever touching the validation card, because nothing forces them through it.

For someone who lives in docuBridge and Vault, the layout itself reads fine — module tabs, section tree, right rail is close enough to what my team knows. But I would have to train nine people on where validation lives versus export, and the fact that those two are in separate cards with no connection between them will generate mistakes. The dossier ID format restriction would trip up every new coordinator on day one.

For me personally this looks manageable — the portfolio page reads like a dashboard my team already keeps in Excel, and the single-column layout means less hunting than Vault's endless side rails. But the correspondence page worries me: if the dossier list fails to load, I'm expected to type an ID by memory in some "e123456" format, and half my team would be stuck right there. Fee status filling in row by row after the list loads would also have people phoning me asking why the fee column is blank.

For me it looks manageable — three flat pages with cards is simpler than digging through Vault workflows, and my team could learn it quickly. What worries me is the correspondence page auto-picking the first dossier; on a busy day someone will log an SDN against the wrong product before their coffee is finished. And if the dossier list fails to load, expecting my coordinators to know the ID format by heart is not acceptable at a CRO managing dozens of client files.

Honestly, the guided journey with locked steps and plain-language blockers would be easy even for my junior associates — easier than docuBridge, which took us months to train on. My concern is the opposite problem: it may be too simplified for a team that files dozens of sequences and doesn't need hand-holding on what Module 3 is. The dossier ID field expecting me to already know the "e123456" format is an odd break in an otherwise beginner-friendly flow.

For me personally, the guided journey with plain-language locked steps would be quite easy to follow — easier than docuBridge, frankly. But my team doesn't need "no regulatory background needed"; we need speed, and I'd worry an eleven-step wizard slows down people who've done hundreds of sequences. The dossier manager also assumes I already know the Dossier ID format, which is an odd mismatch with the hand-holding elsewhere.

Honestly, this looks dead simple — email, password, one card, straight into a dossier manager. My only friction point is the dossier ID field: it demands "one lowercase letter + 6-7 digits" up front, and in real life the dossier ID comes from Health Canada correspondence, so I'd be flipping over to Outlook or our tracker to find it before I can even start. A "don't have your dossier ID yet?" path would save me that dance.

For me this would be trivial — it's a two-field login and a create-dossier form, nothing harder than logging into GlobalSubmit. The dossier ID format validation with an inline example is exactly the kind of guardrail I'd want, since I already have our dossier IDs from Health Canada on file. My only friction point is that if I fat-finger my password there's no forgot-password link, which means a call to IT or the vendor.

Honestly, for me this would be easy — maybe too easy, since it's clearly designed for someone who's never touched an eCTD, and I file ~15 sequences a year. The locked steps would slow me down; in real life I'm working Module 3 content months before I have a Dossier ID confirmed, so a strictly linear wizard fights how submissions actually get built. That said, the "single thing standing between you and ready" callout would save me time versus digging through a GlobalSubmit validation report.

For someone like me who lives in eCTD Office all day, this looks easy — maybe too easy, since it's clearly built for people who've never touched a submission. The locked-step rail and the "single thing standing between you and ready" pointer would actually speed up my triage compared to hunting through validation reports. My only friction worry is the linear 10-step lockstep: I often work modules out of order while waiting on the API vendor, and padlocked steps could get in my way.

For me personally this looks trivially easy — it's a catalog page with tiles and a two-field create form, and I open dossiers all day in eCTD Office. My only friction point is the fixed CS-BE pathway: about a third of my portfolio isn't cross-referenced/BE-only, so I'd hit a wall on dossier three, not dossier one.

Honestly, this looks easier than eCTD Office — two fields and you're into a Module 1 workspace, and the ID pattern validation would catch fat-finger errors before they propagate. My only friction point is that everything hinges on already having the dossier ID in hand; the day I'm setting up a file, that ID request to Health Canada is half the work and this tool just assumes it's done.

Honestly, this looks easier than my current setup — I live in eCTD Office all day and the idea of picking a section in a tree, filling a form, and getting the document generated with the checksum already attached would save me a lot of assembly grunt work. The three-panel layout with module tabs M1–M5 maps to how I already think about a dossier, so I wouldn't need much ramp-up. My only friction point is the "sample" pre-fill — if I'm moving fast on 15 sequences a year, I can absolutely see myself missing one pre-filled field and shipping "Drugazole" boilerplate into a cover letter.

For me this would be easy — the three-panel layout with a section tree, working panel, and status rail is basically how eCTD Office and GlobalSubmit already think, so I'd be oriented in minutes. The M1–M5 tabs and req/opt badges match how I mentally track a sequence anyway. My only friction point is the dossier ID format gate; in real life I don't always have the e-number in hand before I start assembling.

For me personally this would be easy — it's a section tree, an action bar, and a chat box, which is simpler than wrestling with eCTD Office templates. The annoying part is the guessing game: you can't tell from the tree which sections support AI drafting, so I'd be clicking into "Author in-app" section by section just to find out. That's the kind of dead clicking I do enough of in SharePoint already.

Honestly, easier than most authoring tools I've touched — a section tree with req/opt badges and a per-section explainer is exactly how I already think about a dossier. The chat drafting itself is trivial to operate. What would slow me down is having to click into every single section just to discover whether AI drafting even exists for it — with ~15 sequences a year I don't have time to play whack-a-mole across five modules.

For someone who lives in eCTD Office all day, this layout would be easy to pick up — module tabs, a section tree, sequences by four-digit number, purpose chips; it maps to how I already think. My one snag is the dossier ID format gate: I'd have to guess "one letter plus 6–7 digits" until the error told me, which is a dumb speed bump on day one.

For me this would be easy — the layout maps to how I already think: module tabs, section tree, sequences with four-digit numbers. Coming from eCTD Office and GlobalSubmit, running a validation from a card and exporting per sequence is less clicking than what I do now. The only friction is that dossier ID format rule; I'd get it wrong once and then never again.

For someone doing 15 sequences a year this looks manageable — the portfolio rollup and the row-per-dossier layout with gate and fee chips is basically the tracking spreadsheet I keep in SharePoint today. The correspondence page auto-picking my first dossier is fine until the list fails and I'm told to type "e123456" from memory; making the user know an internal ID format is lazy. Three separate pages with slightly different nav chips means I'd be bouncing around more than I'd like.

For someone who lives in eCTD Office and GlobalSubmit daily, none of this looks hard — three single-column pages with obvious cards is simpler than half the tools I use. The fee status trickling in row by row would be mildly annoying on a big portfolio, and the correspondence page auto-picking my first dossier is a small landmine when I've got 15 sequences a year across products — I'd want to be sure which dossier I'm ingesting a notice against before I touch anything.

For me personally this would be easy — honestly easier than eCTD Office, which assumes you already know the CTD backbone cold. The eleven-step journey with locked steps and plain-language unlock reasons would remove most of the "what do I do next" pings I get from junior staff. My only friction point is the Dossier ID entry: I'd want it to pull or request the ID from Health Canada rather than making me type "e123456" from memory.

For me personally it'd be easy — honestly easier than eCTD Office for the assembly mechanics, since the module tree, upload/N/A tabs, and a required-sections counter are exactly the loop I live in daily. The eleven-step journey rail would be training wheels I'd skip past after one submission; I'd want to land straight in the module workspace. The Dossier ID gotcha is annoying though — you have to already know the format before the tool tells you anything useful.

Honestly, the sign-in and workspace setup looks simpler than half the portals I already deal with, so I could get through it fine. The part that would stop me cold is the "New dossier" form — I would not know our dossier ID off the top of my head, I'd have to email my senior or dig through old correspondence to find it. And if I typo my password there's no forgot-password link, so I'd be stuck emailing someone for help.

Honestly, the sign-in and workspace setup looks simpler than half the portals I use — two fields, a create button, done. The part that would trip me up is the "New dossier" form assuming I already know my Dossier ID and its exact format; on my first filing I had to ask my senior what our dossier number even was. If I don't have one yet, I'd be stuck staring at that field.

Honestly, this looks easier than what I do now — I'm still juggling Word templates on the shared drive and asking my senior what order things go in, so a left rail that literally says "You're here" and locks steps I'm not ready for would take a lot of anxiety out of my first filings. The one part that might slow me down is the "Module builder" being a separate workspace — jumping out mid-journey is where I'd get lost.

Honestly, this looks way easier than our current setup of Word templates and a shared drive folder that nobody names files consistently in. The left rail with locked steps would actually help me because I never know what order things are supposed to happen in — right now I just ask my senior. The only part that sounds like it could stall me is the Module builder being a separate workspace; jumping between two screens while a counter counts down missing documents feels like where I'd get lost.

Honestly, this looks easier than our shared-drive Word templates — one button, two fields, and it drops you right into Module 1, which I could figure out without asking anyone. The one thing that would stop me cold is the Dossier ID field: on my first filing I didn't even have one yet, and there's no request step, so I'd be stuck emailing my senior anyway.

Honestly, this looks pretty approachable — labeled fields, an example placeholder like "e123456", and a plain error message telling me exactly what format the ID needs. My worry is what happens before that: the form assumes I already have a real dossier ID from Health Canada, and at my level I'd genuinely be stuck wondering how to get one since there's no request step. The delete "✕" being right on the tile makes me a bit nervous too, even with the confirm dialog.

Honestly, this looks way easier than what I do now — I currently copy old cover letters off our shared drive and pray I changed every product name. The three-panel layout with the section tree feels like the eCTD structure I'm still memorizing, so it would actually help me learn. My only worry is the icons and toggles (Upload vs Author in-app vs Mark N/A) — I'd probably need someone to walk me through it once before I trusted myself to pick the right one.

Honestly, this looks easier than what I do now — right now I'm digging through Word templates on the shared drive and never sure which version is current. The section tree with "req" and "opt" badges and the "required sections complete" counter would tell me exactly where I stand without asking a senior. My only worry is the Dossier ID field — I don't actually know where that ID comes from, and if I get it wrong at step one that would stress me out.

Honestly, this looks easier than what I do now — I basically live in Word templates and email attachments, so a section tree that tells me what's required vs optional would save me from constantly pinging my senior. The chat drafting part feels approachable, like using ChatGPT but pointed at the right section. The one thing that would trip me up is not knowing which sections support AI drafting until I click into each tab — I'd waste time clicking around to find out.

Honestly, this looks easier than what I do now — I basically live in Word templates and email chains, so a chat box that asks me for the details it needs sounds manageable. The one thing that would slow me down is not knowing which sections even support AI drafting until I click into each one; I'd waste time clicking around. But the section tree with req/opt badges would actually help me learn the eCTD structure faster than the folder mess on our shared drive.

Honestly, once I found where things live it doesn't sound too hard — the checkmarks and progress bars are similar to how I track things in my Excel tracker now. But three columns plus a right rail plus module tabs plus chips like "Journey" and "Portfolio" is a lot to take in, and I'd probably need someone senior to walk me through it once before I felt comfortable clicking around a real dossier.

Honestly, this feels busier than what I'm used to — three columns, five module tabs, chips everywhere — but the actual validation part sounds manageable: look at the badge, click "Run full check", read the errors. The sequences card would take me a while though; I've never had to create or manage sequence numbers myself, our seniors handle that, and I'd be nervous picking a purpose from a dropdown without guidance.

Honestly, I think I could figure most of this out on my own, which I can't say for our shared-drive Word templates. The Portfolio page with the big numbers and "Open" links feels straightforward, but the correspondence page has a lot going on — three stacked panels, lifecycle starts, ingest buttons — and I'd probably need a senior to walk me through it the first time.

Honestly, this seems doable for me — it's cards and forms, not some engineering console, and the "Open →" links and empty-state hints tell you where to go next. The correspondence page worries me a bit though: if the dossier list fails to load I'm supposed to just know the ID format on my own, and I'd probably have to email someone to ask what "e123456" means for our products.

Honestly, this looks way easier than what I deal with now — our shared drive of Word templates has nothing like a step-by-step journey telling me what to do next. The locked steps with plain-language reasons would actually help me because right now I'm always asking my senior "can I do this part yet?" The only spot I'd get stuck is the Dossier ID field — I wouldn't know that number off the top of my head on my first filing.

Honestly, this looks way easier than what I do now — our shared drive has like forty Word templates and I never know which version is current. The journey list with locked steps and plain reasons ("Complete Set up your company first") would have saved me so many awkward Teams messages to my manager. The only part that would trip me up is the "New dossier" screen assuming I already know my Dossier ID — on my first filing I genuinely did not know where that number came from.

Honestly, the screens themselves sound simple enough that even I could get through them — two fields, one button, plain labels. My worry isn't clicking through it; it's that I'd be stuck at the very first dossier screen because it assumes I already know a "Dossier ID" in the format e123456, and I'd have to go dig through old correspondence or call our RA consultant before I could even start.

The sign-in and dossier screens themselves look simple enough that even I could manage them — two fields, one button, plain labels. My worry is the parts it assumes I already know, like having the dossier ID and its exact format in hand before I start; in my shop that number lives in a controlled binder and I'd be flipping pages to find it.

Honestly, the guided steps with locked stages and plain-language reasons would suit someone like me — I don't want ten open doors at once, I want one door at a time. My worry is the parts that link out, like the "Module builder" workspace; that's where people in my experience get lost. If it truly walks me through in order, I could manage it without calling IT every hour.

Honestly, the guided step-by-step layout with locked steps and plain-language reasons is something even I could follow without calling IT. I don't love that placing documents happens in a separate "Module builder" window — jumping between two workspaces is where people like me lose track of what's been done. The checkmarks and the "You're here" marker suit how I work through a checklist on paper.

Honestly, this looks simpler than most of the vendor tools I've been demoed — two fields and a create button is something I can handle. My worry is the assumption that I already have the Dossier ID in hand; in our shop that's usually chased down by RA and I'd be entering it second-hand. The little hover definitions would help someone like me who doesn't live in eCTD terminology every day.

For me personally, this looks manageable — two fields, a create button, and tiles I can click. I like that the "Dossier ID" term has a plain-language definition right there, because half my job is explaining these terms to junior staff. My concern is that it assumes I already have a dossier ID in hand with no request step, so I'd still be flipping back to the Health Canada guidance and my paper SOP to get that far.

Honestly, this looks more approachable than I expected — a section tree on the left and a form in the middle is not far off how our vault organizes things. My worry is the sheer number of icons and chips: glyphs, "req/opt" badges, gate flags, module tabs — I would need a good hour with a written user guide before I trusted myself in it. The strict Dossier ID format with a plain-English error message is the kind of hand-holding I appreciate.

For me personally, the three-panel workspace with a section tree and required/optional badges maps closely to how I already track a table of contents on paper, so I could follow it. But there are a lot of little symbols and toggles — status glyphs, "req" chips, AI-versus-sample switches — and at my comfort level I'd need a written SOP and probably a half-day of training before I'd touch a real dossier in it.

The section tree with required/optional badges and status glyphs reads like a checklist, which suits how I already work, so navigating it looks manageable even for someone like me who mostly lives in Acrobat. What would trip me up is only discovering whether a section supports AI drafting after I've opened the tab — I'd waste time clicking around. The chat-style drafting itself seems simple enough, but typing free-form prompts is not something my staff or I have any procedure for.

The section tree with required/optional badges reads like an eCTD table of contents, which I could follow. But finding out whether a section supports AI drafting only after clicking into it would frustrate me — I don't have time to poke around. Typing free-text into a chat box to produce a regulatory document is not how I work; I'd rather fill a structured form.

For someone like me who lives in Acrobat and paper SOPs, three columns of trees, rails, and cards is a lot to take in, but the actual validation piece — a card with a green PASSED badge or a red error count — I could work with that. My worry is the parts around it: I'd need someone to walk me through what "working: 0000" and "Make active" mean before I'd touch them.

Once I found my way to the right rail I could probably follow it, but a three-column workspace with module tabs, chips, and multiple stacked cards is a lot busier than what I'm used to in Acrobat and our vault. I sign off on packages others assemble, so I'd mostly need the validation card and the module readiness flags, and those at least seem to be in one place. The dossier ID format rule would trip me up the first time — I'd have to keep a note taped to my monitor.

For me personally, this looks more approachable than I feared — single-column pages, plain buttons like "Register product +", and forms with clear field labels are within my comfort zone. But the correspondence page auto-picking the first dossier for me, and expecting me to know the dossier ID format if a list fails to load, is the kind of thing that would trip me up and I'd end up calling IT.

Honestly, this looks manageable even for someone like me — three plain pages, one column of cards, no maze of menus. The DIN validation with an example format is exactly the kind of guardrail I'd want my coordinators to have. What worries me is the correspondence page: if the dossier list fails to load, I'm expected to know the ID format myself, and I guarantee half my staff wouldn't.

For someone like me who mostly lives in Acrobat and paper SOPs, the eleven-step journey with plain-language locks actually sounds manageable — it reads like a checklist, and I like checklists. The three-panel layout with a 3D tower spinning on the side is more than I need and would probably distract me. My worry is less the clicking and more that "No regulatory background needed" invites people who shouldn't be assembling a dossier unsupervised.

The plain-language steps and the "You're here" journey would honestly make my life easier than the binder-and-Acrobat routine we run now — I could follow eleven named steps without a consultant translating. But I'd need to know my Dossier ID format cold before I even get in the door, and that "one letter + 6-7 digits" error would trip up half the people I sign off for. The 3D tower does nothing for me; I just want a checklist I can print.

The screens themselves are simple enough — I've filled out worse portals for Health Canada. My concern is the "New dossier" step: it assumes I already have the dossier ID in hand, and for a first ANDS a client won't have one until the Regulatory Enrolment Process assigns it. I'd be stuck at the front door on day one with a new client.

Signing in and creating a dossier looks straightforward enough — two fields, one button, nothing I couldn't manage. My hesitation is the "Dossier ID" field: I'd have to go dig the dossier ID out of prior HC correspondence before I can even start, and half my new clients won't have one yet because HC assigns it. What do I do for a brand-new product with no dossier ID?

For me personally this would be easy — a linear, locked-step wizard with plain-language prompts is far less fiddly than juggling my Word checklists. My worry is it's almost too easy: "No regulatory background needed" makes me wince, because the hard part of an ANDS is not filling in fields, it's knowing whether your comparative bioavailability package actually supports the reference product claim.

For me personally this would be easy — arguably too easy, because it's built for someone with no regulatory background and I've screened these submissions for years. The lockstep left rail with padlocked steps would frustrate me; I often work modules out of order depending on what the client hands me first, and a wizard that won't let me jump to fees or validation until earlier steps clear would slow a practitioner down.

For me this looks straightforward — a tile grid of dossiers, one button to create, and I already keep my dossier IDs in a spreadsheet, so typing "e123456" is no burden. The hover-only tooltip on "Dossier ID" is a small annoyance; I'd rather the 8-week rule be printed on the page than hidden behind a dashed underline I might not notice. Being dropped straight into Module 1 after creation is fine for me, though I usually start by mapping the whole table of contents first.

For me this would be simple — one list, one create form, click into a dossier. The e123456 pattern validation with a plain example is exactly the kind of guardrail I build into my own checklists, so I would not stumble here.

For me this looks manageable — the three-panel layout mirrors how I already think: section tree, working document, status. The dossier ID format validation with an example right in the error message is exactly the kind of guardrail my junior clients need, and the "req/opt" badges save me from cross-referencing my own checklist for every section. My only hesitation is the density of icons and glyphs — I'd want plain-language tooltips because I'm not going to memorize what ⊘ versus ✦ means.

The three-panel layout — section tree, working panel, status rail — mirrors how I already think about a dossier, so I'd find my way around quickly. The dossier ID validation with the e123456 format hint is exactly right and would save sponsors from a common screening bounce. My only worry is form fatigue: I'd want to know how many fields each section really carries before calling it easy.

The section tree with req/opt badges and status glyphs mirrors how I already think about an eCTD table of contents, so navigating would come naturally to me. The chat itself is simple enough, but discovering which sections even support AI drafting by clicking into each one is a time-waster — I manage 6-8 clients and I'm not hunting tab by tab. Typing sponsor details into a chat box is slower than pasting from my own templates in Word.

Mechanically it looks manageable — I live in section trees all day, and the module tabs plus a per-section panel mirror how I organize my own checklists in Word. What would slow me down is hunting: there's no cue in the tree telling me which sections support AI drafting, so I'd be clicking into every section's "Author in-app" tab just to find out. And a two-line chat box is an odd place to draft regulatory prose for someone who spends her day in Word.

The layout itself reads like something I could learn in an afternoon — the three-column workspace and the module readiness flags map roughly onto how I already track a dossier in my own checklists. What would trip me up is the dossier ID gate at creation: "one letter plus 6–7 digits" looks like a Health Canada control number format, but HC assigns those, so I'd be inventing a placeholder just to get in the door. I'd also want to know what "Run full check" is doing before I click it, since "PDF conformance" could mean a dozen things.

The layout itself I could learn quickly — the three-column workspace and module tabs mirror how I already think about a dossier, module by module. My worry is the density of chips and cards; I would want to know exactly where the validation report lives without hunting through a right rail. The dossier ID format restriction would trip up my clients constantly, since real dossier IDs come from Health Canada and people paste them in with stray spaces or wrong casing.

For someone like me who lives in Word and eValidator, single-column cards with plain buttons is manageable — nothing here scares me technically. The correspondence page worries me though: if the dossier list fails to load, I'm expected to know the ID format ("e123456") from memory, and with 6-8 clients I'm not memorizing internal IDs. Auto-selecting the first dossier is actively dangerous in a multi-client practice — I could log an SDN against the wrong sponsor's file before I notice.

For me this looks quite manageable — it mirrors how I already track a portfolio in spreadsheets, one row per dossier with gate and fee status. The correspondence combo box worries me a little: if the dossier list fails to load I have to type an ID like "e123456" from memory, which is fine for me but a trap for my junior clients. I'd want the ingest workflow to be as forgiving as my paper checklists, and it mostly reads that way.

Mechanically it looks easy — an eleven-step rail with plain-language locks is friendlier than anything I had at Health Canada. But easy for a novice can mean slow for me; I don't need "Get oriented," I need to jump straight to Module 2 and the Form 3011 equivalents without a story-mode wizard in my way. The dossier manager assuming I already know the e-number format is fine for me, but it contradicts the "no regulatory background needed" pitch.

Mechanically it looks easy — a numbered journey with locked steps is not far from the checklists I already keep, and I could follow it without training. My worry is the opposite problem: it may be too easy, smoothing over decisions like submission class or reference product that actually require judgment. The "New dossier" form assuming I already know my dossier ID and its exact format is fine for me, but it contradicts the "no regulatory background needed" promise.

Honestly, the sign-in and workspace setup looks dead simple — two fields, a toggle, done. That's my speed; I live in Notion and Google Workspace all day.
